Plotly

Data and libraries

We use the instacart data from p8105.datasets, along with tidyverse and plotly.

library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(plotly)

data("instacart")

The full dataset has over 1.3 million rows. That is fine for plots that aggregate first, but slow for one that draws a point or a box per observation, so we also take a random sample of 50,000 rows. The seed makes that sample reproducible.

set.seed(123)

instacart_sample =
  instacart |>
  slice_sample(n = 50000)

Plotly

Scatterplot

Instacart has no two continuous variables measured on the same row, so a scatterplot needs an aggregation step first. Summarizing to one row per aisle gives us order volume and reorder rate as a pair, and we keep aisles with more than 1,000 items. Volume spans several orders of magnitude, so the x-axis is log-scaled, and text with hoverinfo = "text" replaces the default hover box with a labelled one.

instacart |>
  group_by(department, aisle) |>
  summarize(
    n_items = n(),
    reorder_rate = mean(reordered),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_items > 1000) |>
  mutate(
    text_label =
      str_c("Aisle: ", aisle,
            "\nDepartment: ", department,
            "\nItems: ", n_items,
            "\nReorder rate: ", round(reorder_rate, 3))) |>
  plot_ly(
    x = ~n_items,
    y = ~reorder_rate,
    color = ~department,
    text = ~text_label,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "markers",
    marker = list(size = 9, opacity = 0.7),
    colors = "viridis") |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Number of items ordered", type = "log"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Proportion of items reordered"),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Department")))

Histogram

The distribution of days since the prior order, across all orders with a value. One bin per day gives 31 bins, and bargap adds a little space between them. Note the spike in the final bin: Instacart caps this variable at 30 days, so that bar collects every longer gap as well.

instacart |>
  filter(!is.na(days_since_prior_order)) |>
  plot_ly(
    x = ~days_since_prior_order,
    type = "histogram",
    nbinsx = 31,
    marker = list(color = "#21908CFF")) |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Days since prior order"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Number of items ordered"),
    bargap = 0.05)

Boxplots

Hour of day by department, using the 50,000-row sample. Departments are reordered by median hour with fct_reorder, which makes the ordering meaningful rather than alphabetical, and the legend is switched off because the x-axis already labels each box.

instacart_sample |>
  mutate(
    department = fct_reorder(
      department, order_hour_of_day)) |>
  plot_ly(
    x = ~department,
    y = ~order_hour_of_day,
    color = ~department,
    type = "box",
    colors = "viridis") |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Department"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Hour of day"),
    showlegend = FALSE)

ggplotly

The same aisle-level scatterplot, built in ggplot2 and then made interactive with ggplotly(). Hover text comes from the text aesthetic, which ggplot2 ignores when drawing and ggplotly() picks up.

aisle_plot =
  instacart |>
  group_by(department, aisle) |>
  summarize(
    n_items = n(),
    reorder_rate = mean(reordered),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_items > 1000) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_items, y = reorder_rate, color = department, text = aisle)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  viridis::scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of items ordered",
    y = "Proportion of items reordered",
    color = "Department")

ggplotly(aisle_plot)
